name: Rebellion
miniText: The scientific question is whether local risk perceptions and grievances generate bursts of overt protest. In NetLogo's Rebellion model, citizens compare hardship-based grievance with perceived arrest risk while moving police arrest active rebels. The selected literature connects this mechanism to threshold participation and repression: the explicitly acknowledged civil-violence model supplies citizen-police dynamics [1]; participation thresholds connect individual incentives to collective mobilization [2]; informational cascades provide a historically grounded alternative protest mechanism [3]. Legitimacy, risk aversion and visibility are stylized inputs; the model cannot forecast protest from a grievance slider alone. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

verification.evidenceSummary: This article presents an agent-based computational model of civil violence. Two variants of the civil violence model are presented. In the first a central authority seeks to suppress decentralized rebellion. In the second a central authority seeks to suppress communal violence between two warring ethnic groups.

verification.evidenceSummary: This article analyzes the dynamics of turnout and the political impact of five cycles of protest, consisting of forty-two mass demonstrations that occurred on Mondays in Leipzig over the period 1989–91. These demonstrations are interpreted as an informational cascade that publicly revealed some of the previously hidden information about the malign nature of the East German communist regime. Once this information became publicly available, the viability of the regime was undermined. The Monday demonstrations subsequently died a slow death as their informational role declined.
